3230:
Condense means to make something smaller, shorter, or more concentrated — without losing what is most important about it.

Think of it like squeezing a sponge. The sponge gets smaller, but everything inside it is still there, just packed tighter. That squeezing action — that intelligent compression — is the spirit of "condense."
The Two Main Worlds Where "Condense" Lives

The word works in two broad areas of life: the world of language and ideas, and the world of physical science. Both share the same soul, but play out differently.

1. Condensing Language, Ideas, or Information

When you condense a piece of writing, a speech, or a set of ideas, you shorten it while keeping its core meaning fully intact.

This is not the same as randomly cutting things. When you condense something, you are being smart and deliberate — you strip away the excess, the repetition, and the filler, but everything that truly matters survives.

Examples:

  • A student condenses a 400-page history book into a 2-page summary for revision. The dates, key events, and causes are all still there — just tightly packed.
  • A journalist condenses a 3-hour interview into a 500-word article.
  • Your teacher asks you to condense your essay from 1,000 words to 300 words.
  • A movie trailer condenses a 2-hour film into 2 minutes.

The key point: After condensing, the result should feel complete and sufficient on its own. A reader who only reads the condensed version should still understand the full picture. If important meaning is lost, you haven't condensed — you've just cut carelessly.

2. Condensing in Science and Physics (Gas → Liquid)

In science, condense has a very specific, precise meaning:

When a gas or vapor cools down and turns into a liquid, it condenses.

This is a natural physical process. When something is in gas form, its particles are spread out and moving freely. When you cool that gas, the particles slow down, come closer together, and eventually form a liquid. That transformation — gas becoming liquid because of cooling — is called condensation, and the gas is said to condense.

Examples:

  • In the morning, you see water droplets on the outside of a cold glass. That happened because warm, moist air in the room touched the cold glass surface, cooled down, and condensed into liquid water droplets.
  • Bathroom mirrors fog up after a hot shower because the steam (water vapor) condenses on the cool mirror surface.
  • Clouds form when water vapor high in the atmosphere condenses into tiny water droplets.
  • In industrial settings, steam condenses back into water inside machines called condensers.

The key point here: The gas doesn't disappear — it transforms into liquid. It becomes more concentrated and compact in form. Again, the core idea of "becoming more compact" holds perfectly.
A Deeper Look at What "Condense" Really Implies

When you use the word "condense," you are always communicating two things at once:

① Something is being made more compact or concentrated.
② The essential content or substance is being preserved.

This is what separates "condense" from simply "reduce" or "remove." If you just throw things away, that's not condensing. Condensing is intelligent — you are packing more meaning or more matter into less space.

This is why "condensed milk" (a real product) is called that — it is regular milk with most of the water removed, which makes it thicker, richer, and smaller in volume, but it is still fundamentally milk, just far more concentrated.

Here are natural patterns you'll often see:

  • Condense something into something: She condensed the report into three bullet points. The steam condensed into water.
  • Condense something (by itself): Can you condense this chapter? The gas will eventually condense.
  • A condensed version: He gave us a condensed version of the story. (meaning: shorter, but still complete)
  • Condensed soup: Soup with most of the water removed — you add water back when you cook it.

It helps to know what this word does not mean:

  • It does not mean to summarize sloppily or carelessly. A true condensed version must be faithful to the original.
  • It does not mean to evaporate (which is the opposite — liquid turning into gas).
  • It does not mean to simply delete things at random.

To condense something is to make it smaller or more concentrated while keeping everything that truly matters — whether you're talking about words and ideas, or gas turning into liquid.

Once you see this thread — compacting without losing the essence — you'll recognize the word immediately in any context it appears.
3231:
To condescend means to treat someone as though they are less intelligent, less important, or less capable than you — and to let that belief show in the way you speak to them or act toward them.

It's not just about privately thinking you're better than someone. That's arrogance, and it stays inside. Condescension is when that feeling of superiority leaks out into your behavior toward others.

The word carries two meanings — one modern and dominant, one older and formal.

The modern meaning (what you'll almost always encounter):

To behave toward someone in a superior, patronizing way — to treat them as though they are beneath you in intellect, status, or ability.

"She condescended to her junior colleagues, frequently interrupting them to 'correct' things they hadn't even finished saying yet."

This meaning is negative. The person being condescended to feels belittled, underestimated, or quietly insulted — even if no harsh words were spoken.

The older/formal meaning:

To willingly lower yourself to do something you consider beneath your status or dignity — usually as a gesture toward someone of lower standing, often with the implication that you're doing them a great favor.

"The chairman rarely condescended to attend department meetings."

This older use is less common today, mostly found in older literature or very formal writing. It isn't always meant as an insult — it can simply describe someone important choosing to step down from their position to engage with those below them. But notice: even here, a quiet sense of superiority is baked in. The very word condescend implies the person sees the act as beneath them.

Picture this: You ask a colleague a question about a topic you both know well. Instead of replying normally, they slow down their speech, use very basic words, repeat themselves, and finish with, "Does that make sense?" — as if they're explaining something to a small child.

You understood perfectly. You didn't need any of that. But they've already decided, without checking, that you probably didn't. That quiet sting of being underestimated without cause — that's what condescension feels like from the inside.

Or imagine a doctor who responds to every patient observation with: "That's a sweet thought, but leave the medical thinking to us, alright?" — dismissing the patient as incapable of contributing anything useful. That's condescension in a different form: not loud, not aggressive, but deeply dismissive.

Condescension is often subtle. Rarely does someone announce, "I think I'm smarter than you." Instead, it hides in small behaviors:

  • Over-explaining to experts — going over basic fundamentals with someone who already knows them well, implying they might not.
  • Unsolicited simplification — breaking down something that wasn't complicated to begin with, as if the listener is struggling.
  • Patronizing praise — "Good job!" said to a capable adult who just did something completely ordinary.
  • Dismissiveness dressed as concern — "Oh, you wouldn't understand — it's quite complicated," without actually giving the person a chance.
  • Backhanded compliments — "That's actually a really insightful point — I'm impressed," implying the person doesn't usually say insightful things.
  • Tone — speaking slowly, with deliberate pauses, as if each word needs time to land in a slow mind.

The tricky thing is: the person condescending often doesn't realize they're doing it. They may genuinely believe they're being thorough, patient, or helpful. But to the person on the receiving end, the underlying message is clear: I don't believe you're quite capable enough.
What separates condescension from plain rudeness

Ordinary rudeness is open and direct — "That's wrong," "You don't know what you're talking about." It doesn't hide.

Condescension is more insidious. It is rude while wearing the costume of politeness or helpfulness. The condescending person might never raise their voice. They might smile warmly. They might say, "I'm only trying to help." But the underlying attitude — I'm above you, and I'm generously tolerating your limitations — is still there.

This is precisely why condescension is so frustrating to be on the receiving end of: it's hard to directly confront, because on the surface, the person seems merely helpful or patient. Yet it communicates a quiet disrespect.

Here are the main ways you'll encounter the word:

"to condescend to someone" — to treat someone as inferior.
"He consistently condescended to the interns, as if their questions were a waste of his time."

"to condescend to do something" — to agree to do something you see as beneath your dignity, sometimes reluctantly, sometimes as if granting a favor.
"She rarely condescended to explain her decisions to the team."

Condescending (adjective) — describes a tone, remark, attitude, or manner that carries this quality.
"That was a deeply condescending remark."
"He had a condescending way of nodding while you spoke, as if humoring a child."

Condescension (noun) — the quality, state, or an act of being condescending.
"There was barely disguised condescension in the way she walked him through the steps he'd already completed."

Condescendingly (adverb) — in a condescending manner.
"'That's very brave of you to try,' she said condescendingly."

Condescension is unusual because it is far more visible to the person receiving it than to the person doing it. Someone can condescend all afternoon while genuinely believing they were simply being patient, generous, or thorough.

This means two things:

  1. When you call someone out for being condescending, they may be genuinely surprised — not lying.
  2. It's worth occasionally asking yourself: Am I explaining this because they need it, or because I've already decided they can't handle it without my help? The second impulse, acted upon, is where condescension begins.
3232:
If someone is condescending, it means they behave toward others as if they are superior — smarter, more important, or more capable — and they make that feeling obvious in the way they talk or act. A condescending person, in short, talks down to people.

The key word here is "down." Imagine a tall ladder. A condescending person sees themselves at the top and sees you somewhere far below. When they speak to you, they are not speaking to you as an equal — they are speaking down to you, from their imagined higher position.
What It Looks Like in Real Life

Condescension is not just about what a person says. It is also deeply about how they say it — their tone, their choice of words, and the attitude dripping through their behavior.

Here are some situations that paint a clear picture:

A doctor speaks to a patient and says, "Now, sweetie, I know medical stuff is confusing for regular people, so I'll keep this really simple for you." The patient is, in fact, a biology professor. The doctor did not know that — but even if the patient were not an expert, that tone assumes the person is too dim to handle straightforward information. That is condescending.

A manager reviews a junior employee's report, which is excellent, and says, "Wow, not bad! I'm honestly a little surprised." The hidden message in that "surprise" is: I didn't expect much from you. That unspoken assumption of low ability is condescending.

A person is having a debate, and instead of engaging with the other person's argument seriously, they smile and say, "Okay, that's a cute idea." They are not saying the idea is wrong — they are dismissing it as something a child might say, not worthy of real consideration. That is condescending.

Every condescending act has two ingredients working together.

The first is a sense of superiority — the person genuinely believes, or at least acts as if they believe, they are on a higher level than you, whether in intelligence, experience, class, knowledge, or general worth.

The second is expressing that superiority through behavior — because if someone privately feels superior but treats you with full respect, we would not call them condescending. Condescension only exists when that feeling of superiority leaks out and affects how they treat you.

You can say the exact same words in two completely different ways — one respectful, one condescending. Consider the sentence: "You did well."

Said warmly by a friend or a coach after something genuinely hard, it is encouraging. Said slowly, with a slight smirk, by someone who expected you to fail — as if they are patting a dog on the head — it is condescending.

This is why condescension is sometimes hard to pin down. The words themselves might seem harmless on paper. But the tone carries the hidden message: I am above you.

Common condescending tones include speaking overly slowly to someone as if they cannot keep up, using a soft, gentle voice you would use with a toddler, sighing before explaining something as if it is exhausting to have to explain it to you, or repeating something multiple times in slightly simpler language without being asked to — implying the person clearly did not get it the first time.
It Can Be Intentional or Unintentional

Some people are condescending on purpose. They know they are talking down to someone, and they enjoy the feeling of superiority it gives them, or they use it as a tool to belittle or control others.

But a great many people are condescending without realizing it at all. They genuinely believe they are being helpful. A very experienced professional might over-explain something to a newcomer without noticing they are making the newcomer feel stupid rather than supported. A parent might speak to their adult child as if the child is still twelve years old, not out of cruelty, but out of habit — yet it still lands as condescending to the child.

This is an important nuance: the impact of condescension on the person receiving it is the same whether it was intended or not. Being talked down to feels humiliating, disrespectful, and dismissing — regardless of what was in the speaker's heart.
How It Feels to Be on the Receiving End

When someone is condescending toward you, you typically feel a specific, uncomfortable mix of emotions. There is embarrassment, because you are being treated as less capable in front of yourself (and possibly others). There is frustration, because you know you deserved to be treated as an equal. There is sometimes a quiet anger, because the person did not give you the basic dignity of assuming you are a capable adult. And sometimes, especially if it happens repeatedly from someone in a position of power, there is a slow erosion of your own confidence — you start to believe, against your better judgment, that maybe you really are not as capable as you thought.

This is why condescension, even when "mild," is genuinely harmful.
The Difference Between Condescending and Simply Explaining

A fair question is: is it condescending to explain something carefully to someone who knows less than you? No — absolutely not, and it is important to understand this distinction.

The difference lies in respect. A good teacher or mentor explains things clearly and simply because they respect the learner's ability to understand — they are just providing the context the person needs. A condescending person explains things as if they doubt your ability to understand — the simplification comes from a place of low expectation, not from helpfulness.

Put simply: adjusting how you explain something to suit your audience is a skill and a kindness. Assuming your audience is below you is condescension.

The noun form of this word is condescension — that is the quality or behavior itself ("There was so much condescension in his voice"). The verb is to condescend ("She condescended to her colleagues constantly"). The adverb is condescendingly ("He spoke condescendingly").

The word patronizing is nearly identical in meaning to condescending and can almost always be used in its place. If someone is being patronizing, they are treating you as a child or as someone incapable — talking down to you. The two words are so close that native speakers use them interchangeably in most situations.

Dismissive is a related but slightly different idea — a dismissive person does not take you or your ideas seriously, but they might do so without the strong flavor of superiority that condescension carries. Arrogant is another neighbor — an arrogant person has an exaggerated sense of their own importance, which often leads to condescending behavior, but arrogance is more about how they see themselves, while condescension is more about how they treat others.

If you ever need to recall this word in a flash, remember this: a condescending person treats others as if they are less intelligent or capable, and that attitude shows clearly in the way they speak and behave — they talk down to people rather than talking to them as equals.
3233:
Condescension is the attitude or behavior of someone who acts as if they are superior to another person — and then shows that feeling by the way they speak, behave, or treat that person, making the other person feel small, lesser, or looked down upon.

Think of it this way: imagine someone is standing on a tall step, and instead of stepping down to talk to you as an equal, they lean down from their high step and talk to you as if you can barely understand anything. That leaning-down attitude, that air of superiority disguised (or not even disguised) as helpfulness or politeness — that is condescension.

There are two key parts to condescension that must both be present:

1. A feeling of being superior.
The person believes — consciously or not — that they are smarter, more important, more educated, more experienced, or simply better than the person they're talking to.

2. The outward expression of that superiority.
They show it. This is the crucial part. Condescension is not just a private thought — it spills out into how they speak, the tone they use, the words they choose, or how they behave. And that expression almost always makes the other person feel belittled, patronized, or disrespected.

Without the outward expression, it is just private arrogance. When it is expressed and directed at someone in a way that makes them feel lesser — that is condescension.
What Condescension Looks and Sounds Like

This is where it gets real and vivid. Condescension appears in everyday life in many forms:

  • A manager saying to a capable adult employee: "Good effort! I didn't think you'd actually pull that off." — The hidden message is: I had low expectations of you.
  • An expert talking to a curious beginner and sighing heavily before explaining something, as if the question was too simple to even bother with.
  • Someone explaining how to use a phone to an elderly person by speaking very slowly, in a loud voice, and using baby-like words — assuming the person is incapable, without being asked to simplify.
  • A wealthy person at a party saying to someone: "Oh, you work there? That's... cute. Good for you." — The tone drips with the idea that their own life and work is far more impressive.
  • A teacher correcting a student and rolling their eyes as if to say: "How did you not know this already?"

Notice that condescension is often wrapped in the language of politeness or helpfulness — but the underlying attitude poisons it. The person might smile while being condescending. They might phrase things as compliments. But the sting is unmistakable — you are left feeling as though you have been placed below them.
The Most Important Subtlety: It Can Be Unintentional

This is what makes condescension especially interesting and sometimes tricky. A person can be condescending without meaning to be. They might genuinely think they are being helpful, patient, or kind. But because their underlying belief — "I know better, I am more capable, this person needs my guidance" — leaks into how they communicate, the other person still feels talked down to.

For example, a highly educated person might over-explain something extremely basic to a friend without realizing that the friend already understood it perfectly well. They weren't trying to insult the friend. But the unspoken assumption — "you probably don't understand this, let me simplify it for you" — is still condescension.

This means condescension is judged not just by the speaker's intention but also by the attitude embedded in the behavior itself.
How It Differs from Similar Words

It helps to know what condescension is not, so you can see its exact edges:

  • Arrogance is believing you are better than others — it lives mostly in your own mind. Condescension is arrogance acted out toward a specific person in a specific interaction. You can be arrogant without being condescending in a given moment, but condescension almost always comes from an arrogant attitude underneath.
  • Rudeness is simply bad-mannered or offensive behavior — it can be blunt, aggressive, or careless. Condescension is a specific type of disrespect rooted in a superiority dynamic. A rude person might insult you as an equal. A condescending person talks down to you from an imagined higher position.
  • Patronizing is essentially a synonym — it means treating someone as if they are less intelligent or capable than they actually are. In everyday use, "patronizing" and "condescending" are nearly interchangeable, though "condescension" often carries a slightly broader sense that can include social status, not just intelligence.

If you are on the receiving end of condescension, the feeling is distinct and hard to mistake. You might feel:

  • Infantilized — treated like a child who needs things simplified.
  • Dismissed — as though your intelligence, experience, or opinion doesn't matter.
  • Invisible — as though the person isn't really seeing you, but a reduced, lesser version of you they've decided you are.
  • Frustrated or quietly humiliated — especially when the condescension is dressed up in politeness, because it can be hard to call out.

There is often a particular sting to condescension precisely because it can come from people who claim — and may even believe — that they mean well.

It appears across all areas of life:

  • In the workplace: A senior employee speaking to a junior one as if they couldn't possibly grasp complex ideas.
  • In relationships: One partner constantly explaining things to the other as if they can't think for themselves.
  • In society: Members of a privileged group speaking about or to a less privileged group in a way that implies the latter cannot manage their own lives without guidance.
  • In education: A teacher who makes a student feel stupid for not knowing something, rather than simply teaching them.
  • In everyday conversation: Anyone who speaks with an air of "let me simplify this for your limited mind" — even with a smile.

Here are a few examples of how the noun "condescension" is used naturally:

  • "She couldn't hide the condescension in her voice when she explained the instructions to him."
  • "His constant condescension made every meeting unbearable for his colleagues."
  • "There was a quiet condescension in the way she smiled at his idea before ignoring it entirely."
  • "He dressed up his condescension as helpfulness, but everyone could feel it."

Condescension is the act or attitude of treating someone as if they are inferior to you — expressed outwardly in a way that makes them feel small, talked down to, or unworthy of being treated as your equal.
3234:
Condign means fully and fittingly deserved — particularly when referring to a punishment or consequence. If a punishment is condign, it means the wrongdoer got exactly what they had coming. Not too harsh, not too light. Just right. Justice, served precisely.

Think of it as the verbal equivalent of a perfectly balanced scale of justice: the weight of the wrongdoing on one side, and the weight of the consequence on the other — perfectly matched.

Condign doesn't just mean "fair." It carries a stronger, more emphatic quality. When you call a punishment condign, you're saying: "This person earned this, fully and completely. There is no room for sympathy here — this is exactly what they deserved."

It's a word with a sense of gravity and moral certainty. It feels almost judicial — like a verdict being declared. There's no ambiguity in it.

Condign almost always appears alongside the word punishment. The phrase "condign punishment" is its natural home. You will rarely see "condign" floating freely next to something cheerful or positive. It belongs to the world of consequences, penalties, retribution, and justice.

• "The corrupt official finally received condign punishment after years of abusing his power."

(The punishment he received was exactly what his crimes deserved.)

  • "The court delivered condign retribution for the crimes committed against the innocent."

(The retribution was fitting and fully merited.)

  • "His humiliation in front of everyone was, many felt, a condign consequence for his years of arrogance."

(People felt his humiliation was precisely what his arrogance had earned.)
What Makes It Different From Similar Words

Many words gesture at the same idea, but condign is sharper and more specific than all of them:

"Fair" just means reasonable. A fair punishment could still feel a little light or a little heavy. Condign says the punishment is perfectly proportionate to the offense.

"Deserved" is the closest everyday equivalent, but it's plain and neutral. Condign carries weight — a moral seriousness. Saying a punishment is "deserved" is ordinary; calling it "condign" sounds authoritative and solemn.

"Just" means morally right or correct. Condign goes further — it means not only right, but matched to the specific wrongdoing in a precise way.

"Appropriate" is broader and gentler — it applies to almost any situation. Condign is specifically tied to wrongdoing and its consequences.
The Register: When and Where You'll See It

Condign is a formal, literary word. You won't hear it in casual conversation. You're more likely to encounter it in:

  • Legal or judicial writing
  • Literary fiction, especially older or classic literature
  • Formal essays and criticism
  • History books discussing punishment and justice

It's not a word you'd use in everyday speech — it would sound stiff and unusual. But in writing, especially formal or literary writing, it lands with precision and force.
The One Thing to Always Remember

If you forget everything else, hold onto this:

Condign = a punishment that is exactly, fully, and fittingly deserved.

It is the word you use when you want to say: "They got what they deserved, and there is no argument to be made against it."
3235:
A condiment is a food substance that you add to other food — usually just before eating or while eating — to make it taste better, more interesting, or more suited to your preference. Condiments are not the main food itself; they are extras that sit alongside or on top of the main dish to enhance its flavor.

Think of it this way: when you eat a burger, the burger patty and the bun are the main food. But the ketchup, mustard, and mayonnaise you spread on it? Those are condiments.

Condiments serve one or more of these purposes:

  • Add flavor — Salt, soy sauce, and hot sauce make food taste sharper, saltier, or spicier.
  • Add contrast — A tangy condiment like mustard can balance a rich, fatty food.
  • Add moisture or texture — Mayonnaise or a chutney can make dry food more pleasant to eat.
  • Personalize taste — Condiments let each person adjust the food to their own liking at the table.

The key thing is that condiments are supplementary — they support and improve the main food, but they are rarely the point of the meal by themselves.

Condiments come in many physical forms:

  • Liquid or pourable — ketchup, soy sauce, hot sauce, vinegar, Worcestershire sauce
  • Semi-solid or spreadable — mayonnaise, mustard, hummus, butter (when used as a spread)
  • Chunky or thick — salsa, chutney, relish, pickle
  • Dry or granular — salt, pepper, chili flakes (though these are sometimes called seasonings or spices, they are broadly condiments when used at the table)
  • Paste-like — wasabi, harissa, anchovy paste
Common examples you likely already know

Here are widely recognized condiments from around the world:

  • Ketchup / tomato sauce — paired with fries, burgers, sandwiches
  • Mustard — used with hot dogs, sandwiches, pretzels
  • Mayonnaise — spread on sandwiches and burgers; used as a dip
  • Soy sauce — drizzled on rice, noodles, sushi
  • Hot sauce / chili sauce — added to food for heat and spice
  • Vinegar — used on fish and chips, salads, or pickled foods
  • Relish — a chunky, tangy topping for hot dogs and burgers
  • Chutney — a thick, sweet-spicy sauce common in South Asian cuisine, served with meals, snacks, and bread
  • Salsa — used with tacos, chips, and Mexican food
  • Wasabi — the sharp green paste served with sushi and sashimi
  • Tartar sauce — served with fried fish
  • Pickles / pickle slices — placed inside sandwiches or served on the side
  • Salt and pepper — the most universal and basic of all condiments
When exactly is a condiment used?

Condiments are typically used in one of these situations:

  1. At the table, after cooking — You pour, spread, or spoon the condiment onto your food yourself. This is the most classic use. A bottle of ketchup sitting on a diner table is a perfect example.
  2. During final assembly — When building a sandwich or a burger, you apply condiments as you put it together, right before eating.
  3. As a dip — You dip pieces of food (fries, chips, bread, vegetables) directly into the condiment.
  4. On the side — The condiment is served in a small bowl or dish next to the main food, and you use as much or as little as you like.

Some condiments — like soy sauce or hot sauce — can also be added during cooking, but this does not stop them from being condiments. What defines them is that they are flavor enhancers and not the main food substance.
How condiments differ from similar-sounding things

Since you want to fully understand this word, here are important distinctions:

Condiment vs. Ingredient
An ingredient is something mixed into a dish while it is being cooked or prepared — like onions in a curry or eggs in a cake. A condiment is something added after or separately. That said, the boundary can blur — soy sauce added to a stir-fry during cooking is functioning as an ingredient in that moment, but the same soy sauce at the table is a condiment. The word "condiment" almost always implies the latter use.

Condiment vs. Sauce
A sauce is a liquid or semi-liquid component of a dish — it can be central to the dish (like a pasta sauce). A condiment is supplementary and optional. However, many sauces double as condiments — hot sauce, ketchup, and soy sauce are all both sauces and condiments. All condiments that are liquid can be called sauces, but not all sauces are condiments.

Condiment vs. Seasoning / Spice
Seasonings and spices (like pepper, cumin, or chili flakes) are often used in cooking, but when kept on the table for people to add themselves, they function as condiments. Salt and pepper shakers on a dining table are classic condiments.

Condiment vs. Garnish
A garnish is usually something decorative placed on food (like a sprig of parsley or a lemon wedge). A condiment is meant to be eaten and to add flavor. A lemon wedge can be both — it decorates the plate, but you squeeze it onto your food for flavor, making it a condiment in that moment.

For something to be called a condiment, it generally:

  • Is food or a food substance (not a utensil or anything non-edible)
  • Is added to other food, not eaten on its own
  • Is meant to improve or adjust the flavor of that food
  • Is used in relatively small amounts compared to the main dish
  • Is optional — the meal can exist without it, but it is better (or more personalized) with it
  • Is typically ready to use — you don't need to cook a condiment before applying it (though some condiments are cooked or processed during their making)
Using the word in everyday sentences

Here are natural ways the word "condiment" appears in speech and writing:

  • "Could you bring the condiments? I need ketchup and mustard."
  • "Every table in the restaurant had a small tray of condiments."
  • "She always carries a small bottle of hot sauce — it's her favourite condiment."
  • "The dish was good, but it needed a condiment to give it more kick."
  • "Soy sauce is a staple condiment in Japanese and Chinese cuisine."
  • "The store has a whole aisle dedicated to condiments."

Condiments vary enormously across cultures. What counts as an essential condiment in one cuisine might be completely unknown in another. Fish sauce is a standard condiment in Southeast Asian cooking. Chimichurri is essential in Argentine grilling culture. Mango pickle (aachar) is a beloved condiment across South Asian meals. This global variety reflects the word's broad reach — any culture that enhances food with added flavoring substances has condiments, even if the specific items differ.

A condiment is a flavoring substance — such as a sauce, paste, relish, or seasoning — that is added to food to enhance its taste, usually at the table or just before eating, and is supplementary to the main dish rather than being the main dish itself.
3236: A condition refers to the state something is in or a circumstance that shapes or restricts something. These two ideas — what state and what circumstances — are the two pillars this word rests on. Every meaning of "condition" connects back to one or both of these pillars.
Meaning 1: The State or Quality of Something

This is the most basic meaning. When you talk about the condition of something, you are describing what it is like right now — how good, bad, broken, healthy, old, or new it is.

Think of it as answering the question: "What shape is it in?"

Examples:

  • "The road is in terrible condition." → The road is badly damaged — full of potholes, cracked, rough.
  • "The antique chair was in perfect condition." → The chair looked almost new; nothing was broken or worn.
  • "The patient arrived at the hospital in critical condition." → The patient's health was extremely serious and life-threatening.
  • "He kept his bicycle in excellent condition." → He maintained it very well; it always worked perfectly.

The most common pattern here is: "in [adjective] condition"

  • in good condition, in bad condition, in poor condition, in mint condition, in stable condition.

The word "condition" here works as a report on the current state — like a snapshot of how something is at this moment.
Meaning 2: A Requirement That Must Be Met

Here, a condition is a rule or requirement that must be satisfied for something else to happen. Something is only allowed, possible, or agreed to if the condition is fulfilled.

Think of a condition as a gate. You can only go through the gate if you meet what is required.

Examples:

  • "You can borrow my car on one condition: bring it back by 8 PM." → There is one requirement. If you don't return it by 8, the deal is off.
  • "The company offered her the job with certain conditions." → She had to agree to specific requirements — perhaps about working hours, salary terms, or responsibilities.
  • "He agreed to sign the contract on the condition that his salary would be reviewed after six months." → He set a requirement before agreeing.
  • "The scholarship comes with conditions — you must maintain a certain grade." → There are rules attached to the scholarship that you must follow to keep it.

The key phrase here is: "on (the) condition that..." which means "only if."

This meaning is very common in legal documents, business agreements, negotiations, and everyday promises between people.
Meaning 3: A Medical Problem or Health Issue

In health and medicine, a condition refers to a disease, disorder, or health problem — usually something ongoing or long-term rather than a sudden injury.

Examples:

  • "He has a heart condition." → Something is medically wrong with his heart — perhaps a valve problem, irregular heartbeat, or weakness.
  • "Asthma is a condition that affects the airways." → Asthma is a medical disorder of the breathing system.
  • "The doctor asked if she had any pre-existing conditions before the surgery." → Did she already have any health problems before this treatment?
  • "Living with a chronic condition can be exhausting." → A long-term health disorder that doesn't go away.

Notice that "condition" in this sense is often a softer, more neutral word than "disease" or "illness." Doctors and people use it because it sounds less alarming and covers a very wide range of health problems — from mild to severe, from mental health to physical health.

When you use the word in the plural — conditions — it refers to the overall environment, factors, or circumstances that affect a situation. It describes the way things are around something.

Examples:

  • "Weather conditions were dangerous that night." → The weather — the wind, rain, ice, fog — made it unsafe.
  • "The workers went on strike to protest their working conditions." → The environment they worked in — the hours, safety, pay, treatment — was unacceptable.
  • "Living conditions in the flood-hit village were terrible." → People there had very poor housing, sanitation, food, and basic necessities.
  • "Under these conditions, the experiment simply cannot work." → Given the current circumstances, the experiment will fail.
  • "Economic conditions have improved over the last year." → The general state of the economy — jobs, prices, growth — has gotten better.

Here, "conditions" almost means "the way things are" — the full picture of what surrounds something and affects how it works or feels.
Meaning 5: Physical Fitness (especially "in condition" / "out of condition")

This is a narrower use, but worth knowing. When we talk about a person or animal being in condition or out of condition, we mean whether they are physically fit and healthy — especially for sport or performance.

Examples:

  • "She trained for weeks to get back in condition before the marathon." → She worked hard to become physically fit again.
  • "The athlete was out of condition after months of rest." → He wasn't fit; he had lost his physical readiness.
  • "The racehorse wasn't in condition to run that day." → The horse wasn't healthy or fit enough to compete.

These phrases with "condition" appear very often in everyday English:

  • "on condition that" / "on the condition that" → only if

"I'll help you on condition that you help me back."

  • "under no condition" / "under no conditions" → never; in no situation whatsoever

"Under no conditions should you open that door."

  • "in [adjective] condition" → describing the state of something

Good condition, bad condition, poor condition, excellent condition, critical condition, stable condition.

  • "medical/health condition" → a health problem or disorder
  • "weather/working/living conditions" → the circumstances of an environment

You might wonder: how do all these meanings belong to one word?

They all connect through one underlying idea: "condition" always refers to the state of affairs — either how something currently is, or how something must be.

  • When you describe the condition of a car, you are saying how it currently is.
  • When you set a condition in an agreement, you are saying how things must be for the deal to work.
  • When someone has a medical condition, you are describing the state of their health.
  • When you talk about working conditions, you are describing the state of the environment.

In every case, you are either reporting a state or defining a required state. That is the soul of this word.
3237:
Something is conditional when it depends on a condition — a requirement, a circumstance, or a rule that must be met first. It doesn't stand alone or hold automatically. It comes with a built-in "but only if..." attached to it.

The fastest way to feel this word is to connect it to the word "if." Anything conditional is tied to an "if."

"I will help you if you ask nicely." → The help is conditional.
"She gets the job if she passes the interview." → The offer is conditional.
"The medicine works if taken on an empty stomach." → The effect is conditional.

Remove the condition, and the result may not follow. That dependency is the whole point of the word.

The sharpest way to understand "conditional" is to contrast it with its opposite: unconditional, which means no conditions, no requirements, no ifs. It is absolute and guaranteed regardless of circumstances.

  • Unconditional love = I love you no matter what. Nothing you do can change it.
  • Conditional love = I love you as long as you behave, succeed, or meet my expectations. The love depends on something.

This contrast appears everywhere. Unconditional is a promise without strings attached. Conditional always has strings.

When something is described as conditional, it usually signals that it is not yet final — it can change depending on whether the condition is fulfilled.

  • A conditional job offer or conditional university admission means: "We accept you, but only if you meet certain requirements first" — like getting specific grades, passing a background check, or submitting documents.
  • A conditional loan approval means: "We will lend you money, but only after you satisfy these criteria."
  • Conditional support means: "I support you, but not unconditionally — my support has limits or requirements."
  • Conditional release from prison means: "You can go free, but only if you follow these rules (like reporting to a parole officer)." Break the condition, and you go back.

Notice the common thread: something is being granted or promised, but not freely — only in exchange for meeting a condition.

In language, a conditional sentence expresses what happens if a particular condition is met. These sentences have two parts: the condition (the "if" part) and the result.

  • "If it rains, the match will be canceled." — The cancellation depends on rain.
  • "If I were rich, I would travel the world." — The travel depends on being rich.
  • "If you had studied, you would have passed." — Passing depended on studying.

The "if" part sets up the condition; the other part tells you what follows from it. Neither part can stand alone and give you the full meaning — they depend on each other.

In logic, a conditional statement takes the form: "If P is true, then Q follows."

Example: "If all humans are mortal, and Socrates is a human, then Socrates is mortal."

The conclusion (Socrates is mortal) is not independently guaranteed — it is conditional on the premises being true. This matters in philosophy, mathematics, and any field where precise reasoning is important: many things we accept as "true" are actually conditionally true — valid only when certain assumptions hold.

Conditional probability is the probability of something happening given that something else is already known to be true.

For example: What is the chance of drawing a King from a deck of cards, if you already know the drawn card is a face card? That "given that" changes the calculation. The probability is now conditional on the information you already have. Change the condition, and the probability changes too.

Conditional statements are one of the most fundamental building blocks of code. They tell a computer: "Do this action only if this condition is true."

```
if (temperature > 30) {
display("It's hot outside!")
}
```

The message only appears when the condition — temperature above 30 — is met. This is pure conditional logic: dependent on a test being passed.

Interestingly, when "conditional" is used in emotional or personal contexts, it often carries a slightly guarded or limiting tone — suggesting something is less generous or wholehearted than it could be.

Saying someone gives "conditional friendship" or "conditional kindness" implies there are strings attached, that the warmth isn't freely given. It subtly suggests restriction. But in technical fields — grammar, math, programming, law — the word is completely neutral. It simply describes a logical relationship.

Conditional means: not absolute, not guaranteed on its own — dependent on a condition being met first. Always linked to an "if," always implying that the outcome could differ if the circumstances were different.
3238: To condole means to express sympathy and sorrow to someone who is going through a painful experience — most often the loss of a loved one. When you condole with someone, you are not just feeling sorry for them in your heart silently; you are actively communicating that shared sorrow to them. The word carries a sense of standing beside someone in their grief, telling them: "I feel this pain with you."

Think of it this way: when someone you know loses a parent, you might go up to them and say, "I am so sorry for your loss. I share in your grief." That act — that gesture of reaching out to acknowledge and share in someone else's sorrow — is what "condole" means. It is not just pity from a distance. It is a connection made in a moment of pain.

"Condole" is almost always followed by the preposition "with" and then the person you are expressing sorrow to. You condole with someone. You can also add "on" or "upon" to mention the specific loss.

The structure looks like this:

  • condole with [person]
  • condole with [person] on/upon [the loss or sad event]

• "The minister went to the family's home to condole with them after the tragedy."
    → He visited them to express his grief and sympathy in person.
  • "Friends and colleagues called to condole with her on the death of her father."
    → They reached out specifically to share in her sorrow over that particular loss.
  • "The president sent a message to condole with the nation on the passing of the beloved leader."
    → A formal, public expression of shared grief directed at an entire country.
  • "I could think of nothing adequate to say, so I simply went to condole with him."
    → Sometimes the act of showing up and expressing sorrow is more important than finding the perfect words.
Register: when people actually use this word

"Condole" is a formal word. You will not hear it in casual everyday conversation. People don't walk up to a friend and say, "I've come to condole with you." In real life, people say things like:

  • "I'm so sorry for your loss."
  • "My heart goes out to you."
  • "I'm here for you."

"Condole" appears in formal writing, official statements, news reports, speeches, and literature. A president, a government, a religious leader, or a formal letter would use this word. It has a dignified, respectful weight to it.
How it differs from similar words

It is easy to mix up "condole," "console," and "sympathize." Here is how they differ:

Condole with someone — You are expressing sorrow alongside them. The focus is on acknowledging their pain and showing that you share in it. The emotional direction is with the grieving person.

Console someone — You are trying to comfort them and ease their pain. You are attempting to make them feel better, to soothe them. The emotional direction is toward the grieving person, with the goal of reducing their grief.

Sympathize with someone — You understand and feel for their situation. It's broader and can apply to many situations beyond grief. You share the feeling, but it doesn't necessarily mean you reach out to express it.

A simple way to remember the difference:

  • You condole with someone → you join them in their grief.
  • You console someone → you try to lift them out of their grief.
  • You sympathize with someone → you feel what they feel.

If you have ever heard the phrase "I offer my condolences" or "Please accept my condolences," that is the noun form of this same word. Condolences are the expressions of sympathy you offer. "Condole" is simply the verb — the act of expressing those condolences.

So:

  • The thing you offer = condolences (noun)
  • The act of offering them = to condole (verb)

If you want a single image to remember this word forever:

Picture someone placing a gentle hand on a grieving person's shoulder at a funeral and saying softly, "I grieve with you." That quiet, dignified act of reaching out and sharing in someone's sorrow — that is to condole.
3239:
A condolence is an expression of sympathy and sorrow that you offer to someone who has just experienced a loss — most commonly the death of a loved one. When you express a condolence, you are essentially saying: "I know you are in pain, I feel for you, and I share in your grief."

It is not advice. It is not a solution. It is simply an act of emotional acknowledgment — letting a grieving person know that their pain matters to others and that they are not alone in it.

Condolences are offered specifically in response to loss and grief. The most common situation is the death of someone close — a parent, spouse, child, friend, or colleague. However, the word can also be used for other serious losses, such as a devastating illness, a miscarriage, or even the death of a beloved pet, though this is less common.

You would not use condolences for everyday disappointments like failing a test or losing a job (though those are sad events). The word carries a weight of gravity — it is reserved for deep, profound loss.
Singular vs. plural — an important detail

In everyday English, "condolences" (the plural form) is far more common than the singular "condolence." You will almost always see it in the plural:

  • "Please accept my condolences."
  • "I offered my condolences to the family."

When the singular is used, it usually appears with the word "a" or in formal writing:

  • "He expressed a condolence that felt sincere."

Think of it this way: just as people say "my thanks" rather than "my thank," people say "my condolences" as a set phrase. The plural form has become the standard.
How it is used in sentences

Here are natural examples of the word in real-life contexts:

  • "When her father passed away, her colleagues sent flowers and their condolences."
  • "I called him to offer my condolences after hearing about his loss."
  • "Please convey my deepest condolences to the grieving family."
  • "The president expressed his condolences to the victims' families."
  • "She received hundreds of condolence messages from around the world." (Here, "condolence" is used as an adjective modifying "messages.")
  • "His condolences felt hollow — just empty words without real feeling."

Notice how the word is often paired with verbs like offer, express, send, extend, or convey.
Common phrases built around this word

These are set phrases you will encounter very frequently in real life:

  • "My condolences" — the most common and simple way to express sympathy directly to someone grieving.
  • "My deepest condolences" — a more heartfelt, emphatic version; "deepest" intensifies the sincerity.
  • "My sincere condolences" — stresses that the sympathy is genuine.
  • "Please accept my condolences" — a slightly more formal phrasing, often used in written messages.
  • "A condolence card / condolence message / condolence letter" — a card, message, or letter specifically written to someone who is grieving.
  • "A condolence visit" — when you visit someone in person to offer comfort after a loss.

It helps to understand what the word does not mean:

  • It is not a compliment — it does not celebrate anything.
  • It is not advice — saying "you should be strong" is not a condolence; it is advice.
  • It is not the same as sympathy alone — sympathy means you feel sorry for someone; a condolence is specifically a formal or verbal expression of that sympathy in the context of loss. You feel sympathy silently in your heart; you express a condolence outward.
  • It is not casual — condolences carry a formal, serious tone. You would not say "condolences on missing the bus" as a joke unless you were being deliberately theatrical.

A condolence is a gentle, human gesture. It doesn't pretend to fix anything or take the pain away. It simply says: "I see what you're going through. I care."

When someone has lost a person they loved, there are no words that truly heal the wound. A condolence acknowledges this truth — it doesn't try to make everything okay; it just stands beside the grieving person in their sorrow. This is why condolences are so important: they are one of the few moments in language where we reach out not to inform or persuade, but simply to be present with another human being in their darkest moment.

What it isAn expression of sympathy offered to someone who has suffered a loss
Used forDeath, grief, profound loss
Common formAlmost always used in the plural — condolences
ToneFormal, sincere, serious
Key verbs with itOffer, express, send, extend, convey
It is NOTAdvice, a casual remark, or empty without genuine feeling behind it

Condolence is one of the most human words in the English language — it exists because we need a way to reach out to those who are hurting and say, without pretense: "Your grief is real, and you are not alone."
